To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
E6 abrogates p53 phosphorylation and thereby prevents its cell growth inhibiting activity.
E6 deactivates p53 in HPV infected cells by inhibiting p53 phosphorylation, which prevents p53 binding at the p21 promoter thereby inhibiting p53 cell-growth inhibiting functions.
E6 abrogates p53 function in HeLa cells by inhibiting phosphorylation of p21 promoter binding p53.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms that regulate p53 activity and how these mechanisms are altered by viral proteins to facilitate viral replication.
the mechanisms of inactivation of tumor suppressor p53 by viral oncoprotein E6.
the mechanism by which E6 abrogates p53 function in HPV positive cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
E6 inhibits the phosphorylation of p300 and p53, which results in inhibition of p53 transactivity.
E6 inhibits the cell growth inhibitory function of p53 by inhibits its phosphorylation.
E6 degrades endogenous p53, but inhibits phosphorylation and thereby inactivates p53 overexpression.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
E6 inhibits the phosphorylation of overexpressed wild type p53 and this prevents it from binding to the promoter of p21 and inhibiting cell growth.
p53 is inhibited by E6 by inhibiting its acetylation, phosphorylation and binding to its target promoters.
E6 inhibits the function of p53 in two ways.
The main takeaway from our work is that
E6 does not degrade p53 but inhibits its phosphorylation.
E6 inhibits the phosphorylation of p21, a key regulator of p53.
p53 is not a simple tumor suppressor, but its function is regulated by phosphorylation and E6 inhibits the phosphorylation of p533.
